modes.main: **In a mass-spring system, a mass is attached to a spring, and the pair vibrates around a resting position.** That resting position is **equilibrium**, where the spring is neither stretched nor compressed. The spring always pulls the mass back toward equilibrium. The moving mass tends to **keep moving**, so it overshoots equilibrium and the cycle repeats.
sub: The vibration can be **longitudinal**, which is back and forth along the spring, or **transverse**, which is up and down across it.
Both directions behave the same way, because the same spring pulls the same mass back in each one.
modes.end: So the mass keeps vibrating because the spring keeps pulling it back and the mass keeps overshooting.

modes.main: **The frequency of a mass-spring system depends on its mass and on the stiffness of its spring.** **Frequency** is how many times the system goes back and forth each second. **More mass lowers the frequency, and more stiffness raises the frequency.**
sub: A heavier mass is harder to get moving and harder to turn around, so each cycle takes longer.
A stiffer spring pulls back harder, so the mass returns faster and each cycle takes less time.
modes.end: That is why mass and stiffness push the frequency in opposite directions.

modes.main: **When two masses are joined by springs, the system can vibrate in two different ways, called modes.** A **mode** is one way a system can vibrate. In **Mode 1**, the two masses move together. In **Mode 2**, the two masses move against each other.
sub: In **Mode 1**, the middle spring hardly stretches, so it adds little stiffness and **the frequency is lower**.
In **Mode 2**, the middle spring stretches and compresses a lot, so it adds stiffness and **the frequency is higher**.
The more the masses move **against each other**, the more the springs stretch and compress, so the mode has more stiffness and a **higher frequency**.
modes.end: So a higher mode is a faster mode because more of the springs stretch and compress.

modes.main: **Three masses joined by springs have three modes.** In **Mode 1**, all three masses move together. In **Mode 2**, the middle mass stays still while the outer two move against each other. In **Mode 3**, the middle mass moves against both outer masses.
sub: **A mass changes the frequency only where it moves, and a spring changes the frequency only where it stretches.**
If the middle mass is made heavier, **Mode 1 and Mode 3 go down**, because the middle mass moves in both of those modes.
The same heavier middle mass **does not change Mode 2**, because the middle mass does not move in Mode 2.
modes.end: So Mode 3 stretches the springs the most, because each mass moves against its neighbor, and it has the highest frequency.

modes.ref: Lecture 11 · p7 · Lecture 12 · p7 · Lecture 13 · p3
modes.main: **Every mass added to the chain creates one more mode, so N masses give N modes.** The same patterns repeat as the chain gets longer. Lower modes have broad movements, and higher modes switch direction more often along the chain.
sub: An infinite number of masses and springs along a line is a **string**.
Spread over a surface, an infinite number of masses and springs is a **membrane**, such as a drum or the vocal folds.
A string or a membrane can vibrate in several modes at once.
modes.end: That is why a string and the vocal folds each have a whole series of modes.

springiness.main: **In a vibrating system such as a string or a chain of masses, each spot in a mode is either mostly moving or mostly stretching.** **Where the system moves the most, it stretches the least, and where it does not move, it stretches the most.** So the springiest locations are the points of **no movement**.
sub: The points of no movement are the fixed ends and the points where the mode crosses its resting line.
A **fixed end is always springy** in every mode, because the system cannot move there.
A **free end is always moving** in every mode, because nothing holds it in place.
springiness.end: So moving spots and springy spots take turns along the system.

springiness.main: **A small change at one spot affects each mode according to what that spot is doing in that mode.** Extra mass lowers a mode's frequency **only where that mode is moving**. Extra stiffness raises a mode's frequency **only where that mode is stretching**.
sub: At a spot with lots of motion and little stretching, the extra mass counts, so **the frequency goes down**.
At a spot with no motion and lots of stretching, the extra stiffness counts, so **the frequency goes up**.
Adding mass and stiffness together does **not** cancel out, because at one spot in one mode only one of the two matters. The only exception is a single mass on a single spring.
springiness.end: That is why the same change can raise one mode and lower another.

springiness.main: **Perturbation theory predicts how a small change in one location affects how something vibrates.** In the late nineteenth century, researchers tested this by placing small amounts of wax on different parts of a drum.
sub: When wax was placed where the drum vibrated a lot, the extra mass made the drum vibrate more slowly, so its frequency (pitch) went down.
When wax was placed where the drum did not vibrate, it had no effect on the drum's frequency or sound.
springiness.end: So the wax mattered only where the drum was moving.

harmonics-formants.ref: Lecture 11 · p8 · Lecture 12 · p8, 10 · Lecture 13 · p4, 5
harmonics-formants.main: **A system fixed at both ends, such as a string or the vocal folds, cannot move at either end.** Its first mode is **half a wave** between the two fixed ends. Each higher mode must fit a whole number of those half-waves between the ends.
sub: Mode N contains N copies of Mode 1, so its frequency is N times the first frequency.
These modes at **1, 2, 3, 4 times** the first are called **harmonics**.
If Mode 1 is 200 Hz, Mode 5 is 1,000 Hz.
harmonics-formants.end: So fixed-fixed modes are spaced apart by the first frequency.

harmonics-formants.ref: Lecture 11 · p9 · Lecture 12 · p12 · Lecture 13 · p6 · Lecture 14 · p2
harmonics-formants.main: **A membrane such as the vocal folds vibrates across a surface, and it can vibrate in several modes at once.** One point on the membrane picks up all the modes that move at that point. A **spectrum** separates this combined vibration into its modes.
sub: A spectrum has frequency on the horizontal axis and amplitude on the vertical axis.
It has one spike for each mode that is present. If Mode 1 is 200 Hz, Modes 1 to 6 give spikes at 200, 400, 600, 800, 1,000 and 1,200 Hz.
harmonics-formants.end: So a spectrum shows which modes are present and how strong each one is.

harmonics-formants.main: **A scientific theory is tested by checking whether its prediction comes true.** The theory that the vocal folds are a membrane predicts **equidistant harmonics**, which are evenly spaced harmonics.
sub: To test it, a vowel is recorded and its spectrum is checked in **Praat** to see whether the peaks are evenly spaced.
The recordings showed evenly spaced harmonics, so the prediction was confirmed.
harmonics-formants.end: So the membrane theory of the vocal folds passed its test.

harmonics-formants.ref: Lecture 11 · p11 · Lecture 12 · p14 · Lecture 13 · p7, 8, 9 · Lecture 14 · p3, 4
harmonics-formants.main: **A fixed-free system is held still at one end and free to move at the other.** A **building** is fixed to the ground and free at the top. In the same way, the **air in the vocal tract** is fixed at the closed vocal folds and free at the open lips.
sub: The first mode is a **quarter-wave packet**, which goes from no motion at the fixed end to the most motion at the free end.
The free end must always be moving, so packets are added two at a time, giving one, three, five and seven packets.
So the modes come at **1, 3, 5, 7 times** the first, and these modes are called **formants**.
harmonics-formants.end: That is why fixed-free modes are spaced by **twice** the first frequency, while fixed-fixed modes are spaced by the first frequency.

constrictions.main: **The air in the vocal tract is a fixed-free system that vibrates back and forth along the tube.** It is **fixed at the glottis**, because the closed vocal folds stop the air there from moving, so the air can only be compressed. It is **free at the lips**, where the air moves in and out.
sub: Where the air on both sides moves toward a spot, the air there is compressed. Where it moves away, the air there spreads out.
So the air is compressed the most where it moves the least, and it moves the most where it is compressed the least.
With no constriction, as in **done**, the vowel is **schwa**, and the formants are about **500, 1500 and 2500 Hz**.
constrictions.end: That is why a constriction does different things in different places.

constrictions.ref: Lecture 12 · p16 · Lecture 13 · p12 · Lecture 14 · p8
constrictions.main: **Vowels differ in the shape of the vocal tract, which depends on where the tongue makes a constriction and whether the lips are rounded.** A **constriction** is a narrowing of the tube. With the tongue high and front, the result is the vowel in **dean**.
sub: With the tongue high and back and the lips rounded, the result is the vowel in **dune**.
With the tongue low, the result is an open vowel like the one in **Don**.
constrictions.end: So the same voice from the vocal folds can make different vowels, because each constriction changes the formants.

constrictions.main: **A constriction packs the air into a smaller space, so the air there becomes both heavier (denser) and stiffer.** What the constriction does to a formant depends on what the air at that spot is doing in that mode.
sub: To work out the effect, find the constriction and decide whether the air there is mostly **moving** or mostly **compressed** in that mode.
If the air is mostly moving, the extra mass counts, so the formant goes **down**.
If the air is mostly compressed, the extra stiffness counts, so the formant goes **up**.
constrictions.end: So a large rise in a formant means the air there was springy and hardly moving, and a large fall means it was moving a lot.

constrictions.ref: Lecture 12 · p19 · Lecture 13 · p16 · Lecture 14 · p11
constrictions.main: **For /u/, as in dune, F1 and F2 both go down.** **Lip rounding** makes the constriction at the lips, which is the free end of the tube.
sub: In **Mode 1**, the air at the lips is moving, so the extra mass counts and **F1 goes down**.
In **Mode 2**, the air at the lips is also moving, so the extra mass counts and **F2 goes down**.
constrictions.end: So at the lips only the extra mass matters, because the air there moves in every mode.

constrictions.ref: Lecture 12 · p20 · Lecture 13 · p17, 21 · Lecture 14 · p12
constrictions.main: **For /i/, as in dean, F1 goes down and F2 goes up.** The constriction is about **two-thirds of the way from the glottis**, near the front of the vocal tract.
sub: In **Mode 1**, the air at that spot is moving, so the extra mass counts and **F1 goes down**.
In **Mode 2**, the air at that spot is compressed, so the extra stiffness counts and **F2 goes up**.
constrictions.end: So the formants of /i/ **move apart**, because one constriction sits on a moving spot in one mode and a springy spot in the other.

constrictions.ref: Lecture 12 · p21 · Lecture 13 · p18, 22 · Lecture 14 · p13
constrictions.main: **For /a/, as in Don, F1 goes up and F2 goes down.** The constriction is about **one-third of the way from the glottis**, toward the back of the throat.
sub: In **Mode 1**, the air at that spot is compressed, so the extra stiffness counts and **F1 goes up**.
In **Mode 2**, the air at that spot is moving, so the extra mass counts and **F2 goes down**.
constrictions.end: So the formants of /a/ **move together**, the opposite of /i/.

source-filter.main: **Speech is made by a source and a filter, and the source is the vocal folds.** The vocal folds produce **harmonics** at whole-number multiples of **F0**, the base frequency. With an F0 of 150 Hz, the first five harmonics are 150, 300, 450, 600 and 750 Hz.
sub: Heavy, loose vocal folds vibrate slowly, so they give a **low F0**.
Tight, light vocal folds vibrate quickly, so they give a **high F0**, and the harmonics are spaced farther apart.
source-filter.end: So F0 sets the spacing of the harmonics.

source-filter.main: **The filter is the air in the vocal tract, and its formants decide which harmonics come out loud.** **A formant makes the harmonics closest to it louder, and harmonics far from any formant come out weaker.** The outline of the harmonic heights is the **envelope**, and its peaks show the formants.
sub: The harmonics stay the same from vowel to vowel, and only their heights change.
The envelope is what makes each vowel distinct.
Changing F0 changes the spacing of the harmonics while the vowel stays the same.
source-filter.end: So pitch and vowel are separate, because the source sets the harmonics and the filter sets the envelope.

source-filter.main: **A high F0 spreads the harmonics far apart, so few harmonics fall near each formant.** A low voice has many harmonics close together near each formant, so the envelope shows clearly. A high voice has only a few, so the formants are hard to see.
sub: The vocal tract still has its formants, but there are not enough harmonics near them to show the envelope.
source-filter.end: That is why a toddler's or a soprano's vowels are hard to identify.

source-filter.main: **F0 also carries meaning in speech.** F0 falls at the end of a statement and rises at the end of a question.
sub: F0 also signals sarcasm or pretending.

spectrogram.main: **A spectrum shows a sound at one instant, and a spectrogram lines up many spectra over time.** In a spectrum, frequency is on the horizontal axis and amplitude is on the vertical axis. In a **spectrogram**, time is on the horizontal axis, frequency is on the vertical axis and **darkness** shows amplitude.
sub: The **dark bands are the formants**, because the harmonics near each formant are the loudest.
F1 is the lowest dark band, and F2 is the next one up.
spectrogram.end: So the bands rise and fall as the vocal tract changes shape.

spectrogram.main: **Each vowel moves the formant bands away from schwa in its own direction.** From schwa to /i/, the bands **move apart**. From schwa to /u/, **both bands drop**. From schwa to /a/, the bands **move together**.
sub: Going from /i/ to /a/, F1 rises and F2 falls.

spectrogram.main: **In connected speech the formants never stay still, because every sound moves the constriction.** In "Where were you a year ago?", F2 rises when the tongue moves toward /i/. The formants drop when the lips round for the /u/ of you.
sub: When the tongue moves back and down toward an /a/-like sound, F1 rises and F2 falls.
spectrogram.end: So speech is a continuous series of constrictions, not a list of separate vowels.

spectrogram.main: **Listeners identify a consonant partly from the vowel after it.** In **Malécot**'s work in the 1950s, the m of ma was joined to the a of na. Listeners heard na.
sub: The vowel from na still carried the formant transition left by the n, and listeners used that transition.
spectrogram.end: So listeners decide on the consonant during the vowel, after the consonant is over.

network-forward.main: **The vowel network is a neural network that takes a vowel as two numbers and picks a word.** Its inputs are **F1 and F2**. It decides among five words, **done, dune, dean, Don and Dan**.
sub: A low F1 and a high F2 is /i/, so the right answer for that input is dean.
network-forward.end: So the whole network turns two formant values into one choice among five words.

network-forward.main: **Each neuron in the network multiplies each incoming activation by its weight and adds the results.** This sum is the **inner product**, the core calculation of all AI. A **weight** is a positive or negative number that sets how much an input counts.
sub: A positive weight keeps the input's sign, and a negative weight flips it.
**The network's knowledge is stored in its weights**, so learning means changing the weights.
network-forward.end: The weights start out random and become useful through learning.

network-forward.ref: Lecture 14 · p24 · Lecture 15 · p3 · Lecture 16 · p3
network-forward.main: **Forward propagation carries the inner products layer by layer from the input to the output.** The input layer supplies F1 and F2. Each later layer takes the activations from the layer before and passes its results on.
sub: The output layer gives one number for each of the five words.
network-forward.end: So a forward pass makes a guess with the current weights, even when the weights are not learned yet.

network-forward.main: **The output of the vowel network is a probability distribution over the five words.** Each number is between 0 and 1, and the numbers **add up to 1**. The largest number is the network's decision.
sub: The right answer is written as a **one-hot** list, with 1 for the correct word and 0 everywhere else.
For dean, the one-hot list is 0, 0, 1, 0, 0.
network-forward.end: So a guess can add up to 1 and still put the most probability on the wrong word.

network-forward.main: **The direction of a change in an output follows from the signs of the activation and the weight.** A positive activation times a positive weight is positive. So raising either one pushes that output's probability **up**.
sub: With a negative weight, the same input pushes that output's probability **down**.

backprop.main: **Every neural network starts with random weights and learns by correcting its mistakes, one small step at a time.** **Backpropagation** is the method that works out how each weight should change. **The last set of weights is updated first, and the first set of weights is updated last.**
sub: The last weights affect the output probabilities **directly**, so one inner product shows whether each should go up or down.
A first-layer weight affects the first hidden layer, which affects the next layer and the next.
So the effect of a first-layer weight passes through every layer and depends on all the later weights.
backprop.end: That is why learning starts at the end and works back toward the input.

backprop.main: **Dynamic programming solves the easy problem first and reuses its answer for the bigger problem that contains it.** This idea comes from **Bellman** and **Viterbi**. In backpropagation, the easy problem is the last layer, and the bigger problem includes every earlier layer.
sub: **Backpropagation is stochastic gradient descent plus dynamic programming.**
Stochastic gradient descent (**SGD**) changes each weight a little, and dynamic programming sets the order of the changes.

backprop.main: **Backpropagation was worked out in the mid-1980s.** Geoffrey Hinton won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics for it.
sub: The idea is at the center of much of today's economy.

pytorch.ref: Lecture 14 · p22 · Lecture 15 · p2 · Lecture 16 · p2
pytorch.main: **The vowel network is written in PyTorch as a short list of layers.** The network has 2 inputs, three hidden layers of 3, 2 and 4 neurons, and 5 outputs. The 2 inputs are F1 and F2, and the 5 outputs are the five words.
sub: The import lines bring in the **torch library**, which already contains the programs for inner products and backpropagation.
So none of that math has to be written by hand.

pytorch.main: **In the code, nn.Sequential means the network is a sequence of layers, one after another.** Each nn.Linear line is a processing layer that computes inner products. **nn.Linear(2, 3)** takes input from 2 neurons and has 3 neurons.
sub: The first number on each line must equal the second number on the line before it. The vowel network has Linear(2, 3), Linear(3, 2), Linear(2, 4) and Linear(4, 5).
The **input layer gets no line**, because it does no processing, and the **last line is always the output layer**.
nn.Sigmoid lines are not layers, so they are not counted.
pytorch.end: So the four Linear lines are the three hidden layers and the output layer.

pytorch.main: **The training lines make a guess, measure the mistake and change the weights.** **SGD** is stochastic gradient descent, and **lr** is the learning rate. The **loss** is the mistake.
sub: **backward** runs backpropagation, and **step** updates the weights.
**A higher learning rate learns faster but less accurately, and a lower one learns more accurately but more slowly.**

sigmoid.main: **The sigmoid is a function that takes a neuron's inner product and returns a number between 0 and 1.** A large negative input gives about **0**, which is off. A large positive input gives about **1**, which is on. An input of exactly 0 gives **0.5**.
sub: The curve is flat at both ends and steep in the middle, so the same change in the input matters most near the middle.
Very different things can be perceived as the same, such as a friend with or without a hat, just like the flat parts of the sigmoid.
Very similar things can be perceived as different, such as USC and UCLA, just like the steep middle of the sigmoid.

sigmoid.main: **In the code, nn.Sigmoid goes after each hidden layer.** Each hidden neuron first computes its inner product and then applies the sigmoid. The sigmoid's output is what goes to the next layer.
sub: The last layer has no sigmoid, because its outputs go to the loss, which turns them into probabilities.
Hidden sigmoid values are each between 0 and 1, but they do not have to add up to 1, so they are not a probability distribution.
sigmoid.end: So when a sigmoid changes a hidden value, every later layer changes too.

sigmoid.main: **The sigmoid comes from a discovery about real neurons.** **Lord Edgar Adrian** won the Nobel Prize in 1932 for showing that **neurons are nearly digital**, either firing or not firing. The sigmoid behaves the same way, because its output is nearly off or nearly on.
sub: Many basic ideas in AI, including neurons, inner products and near-digital firing, come from discoveries about real brains.

training.main: **The vowel network is trained on a table of real vowel recordings, and each row of formants is paired with its vowel.** The input table has two columns, F1 and F2. The target table has five columns, one for each word.
sub: For dean, the target row has a 1 in the dean column and 0 everywhere else.
If the rows got mixed up, the network would learn the wrong word for those formants.

training.main: **When the F1 and F2 of real speakers are plotted, the vowels overlap a lot.** Each dot is one recording. Recordings with nearly the same F1 and F2 can be different vowels.
sub: **Peterson and Barney** found this overlap in the early 1950s.
Even a person would have to guess for a point in the middle of the overlap.
training.end: So one pair of formants does not always point to one vowel.

training.main: **Accuracy is how often the network picks the right word, and it starts at chance.** With random weights the network knows nothing. A random guess among **five** vowels is right one time in five, so accuracy starts at **20 percent**.
sub: With ten categories, chance would be 10 percent.
Each pass of learning is an **epoch**, and a problem like this takes thousands of them.
The network jumps to about 40 percent and levels off near **45 percent**, because the real vowel data **overlap** so much.

training.main: **Ten training runs that start from different random weights take different paths but end at the same accuracy.** Each run begins with its own random weights, so each one learns along its own path.
sub: Children are similar, because they hear different input but learn the same language.

training.main: **Children learning English first use forms from memory and later learn the pattern behind them, as Carol Chomsky observed.** At first, children say went correctly by memory. Then they say goed after learning the pattern.
sub: Later they learn that went is an exception to the pattern.

lead-up.main: **A neuron in an artificial neural network takes in a vector and gives back one number.** It multiplies each input by its weight and adds the results, which is the **inner product**. A **neural network** repeats the inner product layer after layer.
sub: A neural network takes in one vector and gives back a vector of decisions.

lead-up.main: **Artificial neural networks began in biology, not in technology.** The first paper on artificial neural networks, by **McCulloch and Pitts**, started from the all-or-none behavior of real neurons. A neuron is either firing or not firing, which is the same idea as the **sigmoid**.
sub: The earliest neural network work tried to model how the mind works, including mental illness.
In the **Parallel Distributed Processing** books, **parallel** means many neurons calculate their activations at the same time.
**Distributed** means the information from the inputs is spread across all the neurons. By the time of these books, forward propagation and backpropagation were well worked out.

lead-up.main: **The vowel network takes one static vector and makes one decision.** A **static** vector is a fixed list of numbers from one moment. Speech changes all the time, and a sentence is many words one after another.
sub: So one fixed list of numbers cannot model thinking that unfolds over time.

lead-up.main: **A recurrent network sends its own output back into part of its input, so what it produces at one moment helps predict the next.** **Michael Jordan** built the **recurrent** network to model speech production. He built it because features such as nasality and lip rounding switch on and off at different moments.
sub: **Plan units** and **state units** feed the hidden layer, and the hidden layer feeds the output.
The output is copied back into the state units, and the same weights are used at every step.
lead-up.end: So a recurrent network can work through a sequence instead of one static vector.

lead-up.main: **GPT works the same way as the recurrent network, one word at a time.** It predicts the next word and adds it to the prompt. Then it feeds everything back in to predict the word after that.
sub: The years 1943, 1985 and 2017 mark the main steps in this history.

heads-layers.main: **An LLM is built from layers, and each layer contains heads.** A **layer** is one round of improvement, and layers go one after another from the input to the output. A **head** is one expert, and it is a set of weights. Heads sit side by side inside each layer.
sub: Each head gives its own opinion on how to improve the vectors.
The layer combines all of the heads' opinions into improved vectors, and the next layer then does the same thing again.

heads-layers.main: **Heads and layers work like visiting a series of classes to improve yourself.** The classes you visit one after another are the **layers**. The students in each class who each give you an opinion are the **heads**.
sub: Layers give an LLM **depth**, which is one round of improvement after another.
Heads give an LLM **width**, which is many experts asked at the same time in each round.

heads-layers.main: **Predicting the next word is so hard that large systems have a hundred or more layers with about a hundred heads in each.** Every one of those heads learns.
sub: If the predicted next word is wrong, every head in every layer adjusts its weights with backpropagation. So the next prediction is closer to the right word.

llm-sequences.main: **An LLM is given a sequence of vectors and predicts the next one.** It is given 15 vectors and predicts the sixteenth. The sixteenth is a probability distribution over what could come next, such as each of about 30,000 English words.
sub: The vectors can be words, frames of a spectrogram, patches of an image or the amino acids of a protein.
The LLM only ever sees lists of numbers, so the same design works for all of them.

llm-sequences.main: **Language depends on connections between words that are far apart.** In "the dog that my parents, who I love very much, ...", the next word is **barks**. Barks goes with the singular dog, no matter how many words come in between.
sub: An LLM learns this from data, not from a taught rule.

llm-sequences.main: **An LLM learns by predicting the next word, such as mat after "the cat sat on the".** When the prediction is wrong, backpropagation adjusts the weights. This is repeated with a huge number of sentences.
sub: Underneath everything, inference is inner products, and learning is stochastic gradient descent plus dynamic programming.
An LLM predicts from past data, so something its data does not cover can make it make things up, which is called **hallucination**.

gestalt-cloze.main: **Gestalt psychology studies how people see whole patterns.** People see a triangle in the Gestalt figure even though no triangle is drawn. They see it because a large part of human knowledge is completing what is missing.
sub: **Closure** is the Gestalt word for completing a familiar pattern that is not quite finished, such as seeing a broken circle as whole.

gestalt-cloze.main: **In a cloze test, words are removed from a text and people fill them in.** The name comes from closure. The test measures knowledge by asking someone to complete a sequence.
sub: An LLM predicting the next word is playing a cloze game again and again.
gestalt-cloze.end: So training a system only to predict the missing piece turns out to copy human thinking.

recurrent-dynamical.main: **A dynamical system is a rule that is fed its own output again and again.** Numbers go in, the rule acts on them, and numbers come out. The output then becomes the next input.
sub: In the **harmonic oscillator**, the two numbers are position and velocity, and they take turns updating.
Step by step, the rule draws a **cosine**.

recurrent-dynamical.main: **An LLM can be treated as a dynamical system.** Each layer is the rule, and the depth of the layers plays the role of time. The input vectors are the **initial conditions**.
sub: Each layer turns the vectors into better vectors until the last layer can predict the next word.
Each layer has its own learned weights, so one step feeds the next without using the same numbers at every step.
recurrent-dynamical.end: So in both systems, the output of one step is the input to the next.

agentic.main: **An agentic system is a group of LLMs connected so that one LLM's output becomes the next one's input.** An **agent** in AI today is just an LLM. In one example, an outline LLM plans the answer and a writing LLM writes it.
sub: A critic LLM checks the draft, and a revision LLM works back and forth with the critic.
A final LLM produces the answer the user sees.

agentic.main: **The critic loop sends the draft back and forth between the critic and the reviser.** The loop continues until the critic is satisfied or a limit is reached. This loop greatly reduced hallucination.
sub: Once each LLM is trained, its weights usually do not change.
The agents share a common memory, where they write and read information.

agentic.main: **Software 1.0, 2.0 and 3.0 are three ways to build a program.** **Software 1.0** is writing a program in a language such as Python. **Software 2.0** is training a neural network on input and output data, so the program is its weights.
sub: **Software 3.0** is having an agentic system build and run the program from plain English instructions.
Building a program this way is called **vibe coding**.

phonotactics.main: **Phonotactics are the rules for which sounds can follow which in a language.** Every speaker knows them without being taught. A simple English syllable is a consonant, a vowel and a consonant, as in **Don** or **cup**.
sub: Mat, sit, dog, fish and shave are also consonant, vowel, consonant.
The pattern is about sounds, not letters, so the silent e of shave does not count.
Ship, chin and bath also count, because sh, ch and th are each one sound spelled with two letters.

phonotactics.main: **Consonants can also form clusters before or after the vowel.** A cluster before the vowel is an **onset**, as in split, flat, black and glad. A cluster after the vowel is a **coda**, as in desk, help, milk and lamp.
sub: The order is a mirror image around the vowel, so flat is a word and lfat is impossible.
Each real word has an impossible twin that puts the wrong consonant next to the vowel, such as help and hepl, or lamp and lapm.
Sblit and desb are impossible too, which is why a product called desb would sound un-English.

phonotactics.main: **A pair of consonants can be fine across a syllable break and impossible at the start of a syllable.** Atlantic is a word because t and l are on opposite sides of a syllable break. Tlantic is impossible because tl cannot start an English syllable.
sub: The sound ng can end a syllable but never start one.

phonotactics.main: **Each language has its own phonotactics.** Mandarin allows only nasal sounds at the end of a syllable. Russian and Polish allow clusters like zb or dl at the start of a word.
sub: Spanish speakers add an e before st at the start of a word, as in estadio.

phonotactics.main: **Guessing the next letter of a word depends on phonotactics, and each guess is a probability distribution.** After a vowel, almost any letter can come next, so the distribution is **flat**. At the start of a word, the choices narrow to what an English onset allows.
sub: After ra, almost any letter can come next, such as t, n, r or l, so the distribution is flat.
After skr, the distribution is **sharply peaked** on a few vowels.
phonotactics.end: So a GPT trained only on this game learns English syllable structure, because guessing the next letter is predicting the sixteenth item.

phonotactics.main: **At the start of a word, each first letter or cluster allows only a few next letters.** After sp, only l, r or a vowel can come next, never n. After k, a vowel or n can come next, as in knee, but never t.
sub: After b or f, only r, l or a vowel can come next, never n.
After sh, only a vowel or r can come next, as in shrimp.
After skr, or after m at the start of a word, only a vowel can come next.

phonotactics.main: **Inside a word, the letters so far can make one next letter almost certain.** After bram, the letter b is almost certain, as in bramble.
sub: A new syllable could also start there, so b is not the only possible next letter.

phonotactics.main: **After pl, st and th at the start of a word, the next letter is limited too.** After pl, only a vowel can come, as in play. After st, a vowel or r can come, as in star and street, but not l or k.
sub: After th, r, w or a vowel can come, as in three, thwart and thin, but not l or n.
